Copper Quarterly Report January 2010 

# Executive Summary Asia-centric future 



- **Chinese demand** growth continues to drive our forecast, with copper consumption growth now broad-based and primarily domestically generated **.** This will equate to a further 3Mt increase in Chinese refined copper consumption between 2009 and 2014. 



- **Prices** will be supported in the short term by a **lag in scrap supply** , as industrial production and construction activity in developed markets remain well below pre-crisis levels, combined with a limited primary supply response in 2010 (output flat compared to 2009). Furthermore, we believe **investors will support prices** unless the economic picture turns decidedly worse.  By 2011, Chinese refined consumption growth will decelerate to single digits, but consumption growth in developed markets will provide a fillip to cathode demand. 



- In the medium term, we see a **balanced market** moving towards deficit, driven by continued and sustainable consumption growth, led by China.  This will be met by a supply side push in 2011-2013 driven by a strong cash flow and a return of risk appetite. 



- However, the economic downturn means the **project pipeline is insufficient** to meet demand growth by 2014.  The majors control many of the best projects, but will remain cautious in order to protect cash flow.  Thus, by the end of our forecast period the supply side will be moving back to 2007/08 conditions (when growth was constrained by a lack of people and equipment), pushing the market back towards deficits.  Continued high copper prices and constrained supply could result in **accelerating substitution or rationing** in low value added (non-electrical) applications. 



- Over our forecast period the world of **copper is changing to an Asia-centric world** .  China will become self sufficient in semis production, putting pressure on semis exporters elsewhere, while the rest of Asia and Middle East will see solid consumption growth.  The Chinese smelting industry will look to supply as much of the copper required by its domestic semis industry as it can.  The resulting growth in Chinese smelting capacity will keep TC/ RCs from rising much, putting financial pressure on other smelters that may lead to closures.

The main driver has been a higher scrap replacement effect, but also higher copper semis growth. **Supply** : Our refined production estimate for 2009 is almost 400,000t higher, due to disruptions and negative impacts of smelter acid demand turning out to have been less than previously expected. A higher mine production forecast and estimated scrap usage in smelting/refining has also raised our forecasts of refined production between 2010 and 2014 by an average of 160,000t per year. **Prices** : Given the above, average prices are $1,420/t higher in 2010 and $425/t in 2014. ### Supply struggles to keep pace with recovering demand There were relatively small increases in supply in 2009 throughout the year, with the build up in inventories eventually accelerating over the last quarter of the year. Meanwhile, this has not prevented prices trading up at levels of around $7,500/t in the first few weeks of the New Year. These higher prices are helping the smaller producers/explorers to raise money again, with a marked increase in copper deals in December 2009. However, these prices have brought back a differential with competing products, particularly aluminium, which means substitution threats away from copper will return as an issue. In 2010, there will be little additional refined production due on stream given the dearth of projects. This year will hopefully see the world move out of recession and transition into more favourable economic conditions, which means demand for refined metal shows no signs of abating from the developing world and China in particular. This will lead to a slight deficit this year, which will support prices at current levels. for copper. Demand growth will continue at pace in 2010 supported by robust growth of 13-15% in semis production, fuelled by the ongoing structural factors in new semis capacity coming on stream that is "refined intensive". In addition, semis production growth will be sustained by the structural shift of Chinese semis output replacing imports of semis from overseas. This is particularly relevant in wirerod and the sheet and strip sectors. What is also clear is that the brass mill segment is now following the early recovery in the wirerod and wire & cable sector. This is all being supported by growth in end use markets. Although prospects were patchy earlier in the year, the data is now turning and the signs are very strong; e.g. November automotive production rose 101% y-o-y, air conditioners were up 58% y-o-y, laptops +64% y-oy, integrated circuits +42% y-o-y, mobile phones +46% y-o-y, electric motors +7% y-o-y. The construction picture is improving briskly too. Admittedly, the year-on-year comparisons are being magnified somewhat by the tumble that began in late 2008 when the global credit crisis first got underway. However, it seems to confirm that China has completed restocking all the way through the supply chain and that continued copper consumption growth is justified by end use sector growth. Exports have also been growing sequentially (in semis, wire & cable and finished goods). All the signs suggest that consumption growth in China is now broad-based, with all segments contributing to the continued recovery rather than the narrow, specific factors that ignited the early recovery in 2009. Indeed, the Dubai debt drama that came to light late in November 2009 was a timely reminder of the fragility of the global financial system. It highlights a protracted recovery that will be delicate. The degree (or absence) of a recovery in the world economy this year will determine the demand prospects for copper. Our growth in 2010 is driven by China and the rest of Asia, with muted support from Europe and North America. If the latter regions recover faster than expectations, this will support higher copper demand growth. The scrappage schemes in 2009 have brought forward production in the automotive sectors which will benefit demand for copper in H1 2010. A recovery in manufacturing activity should spur growth over the second half of the year. The recovery is tenuous, however, and many copper consumers remain unwilling to restock given the lack of clarity in the order pipeline. The high prices of raw materials could delay any restocking-led recovery further and could stall demand growth which is only just starting to

show signs of improvement. 

Globally, we do not expect to return to 2007/08 levels of refined copper consumption before 2011.  However, what is clear is that total refined copper consumption will now be heavily represented by Asia, the Middle East and North Africa, which together account for around 65% of the total.  This is an increase of 10% compared to 2007, driven by the advanced recovery in Asia, and augmented by the structural shifts in China highlighted above.  This change in the market’s centre of gravity also reflects the dwindling significance of Western Europe and North America as power houses of refined copper consumption growth and highlights the impact of off-shoring and out-sourcing that is unlikely to be reversed. 

### Production to bounce back, but… 

Production in 2009 turned out to be higher than our forecasts for both mine and refined, as a result of limited disruptions across the production chain.  In addition, smelter cutbacks were less than expected as a result of the sulphuric acid market correcting more quickly than previously forecast.  Mine production surprised on the upside during 2009 despite a couple of setbacks, including the outage at Olympic Dam and the SAG mill closure (and lower ore grades) at Escondida.  Most of the labour agreements that were due for negotiation last year passed with little disruption.  The only exception was the 42 day strike at BHP Billiton's Spence mine in Chile in October 2009, with an estimated loss of 35,000t of EW copper cathode. 

Mine production growth, however, is set to remain insipid this year with very few new projects due on stream, and those that are, are only expected to contribute a paltry 45,000t.  The only greenfield project of any notable size is Antofagasta’s Esperanza, which is due on stream during the fourth quarter of this year and will ramp up to its 191,000t capacity by 2011.  A further 390,000t should come from brownfield expansions and restarts. 

In the concentrates market, smelting capacity growth, especially in China, is set to continue to outpace that of mine output.  The concentrates market was more or less balanced for 2009, registering a small deficit of 42,000t.  Nevertheless the lack of sufficient raw material will keep the concentrates market in deficit again in 2010 and should maintain the pressure on the smelting industry to rationalise and will be a key factor determining refined copper production. Indeed, the first contract for 2010 has been settled at terms of $46.5/4.65¢/lb, 40% lower than terms for 2009 delivery.  This is below breakeven levels for the Japanese, although smelters

Much of the increase in the new concentrate processing capacity will be owned by already established producers, Tongling Group, Yunnan Copper, Zhongtiaoshan and Huludao, which already have existing sources of supply and therefore are likely to encounter fewer difficulties in sourcing additional raw materials. 

Nevertheless, the additional concentrate requirements will put further pressure on already tight concentrate and scrap markets, and it is unlikely that all of this new tonnage will be able to secure sufficient material to operate at planned levels, or even at all during the outlook period. In order to ensure sufficient feed of raw material the Chinese are continuing to invest up stream with their most recent venture in Corriente Resources, securing the 62,000tpy Mirador project in Ecuador which is due to start up in 2013. 

Smelters, particularly those in China, predict that raw material availability, both scrap and concentrates, will be the key factor determining production rates this year, rather than the sulphuric acid market that affected output to some degree through 2009.  The acid market has become less of an issue; the market is looking more balanced and threats to smelter production seem to have receded for the time being.  It has become more of a revenue issue for the smelters as prices are low.  For example, Codelco has agreed $35-65/t for its acid compared with $110140 in 2009 and $180-200 in 2008. 

The Chinese also continue to invest heavily in secondary facilities.  According to our research and based on known plans, Chinese refined production from scrap would more than double from 2009-201

4 given sufficient scrap availability. The scrap market will improve as the economic recovery gains momentum. We have assumed some recovery in 2010, with higher growth in 2011 and 2012. We have applied a raw material adjustment to global scrap production, and have assumed that most of the adjustment will occur in China. As a result we estimate a 75% increase in production in China from 1.3M tonnes to 2.3M tonnes by 2014. We have also assumed that production will take an increasing share of the total scrap consumed in China and away from the semis sector. ### …projects not expected to ramp up enough to boost stocks The buoyant copper prices and strong demand have encouraged the development of a number of copper projects, but with investors still wary following the financial collapse of 2008, the projects that are moving ahead are not the most risky of ventures. Brownfield operations are popular due to their inherent existing operations and infrastructure, familiar geology and workforce arrangements which present fewer potential surprises as things progress. By 2014, brownfield projects will account for some 40-45% of the forecast production from new projects, including committed, probable and possible. Amongst greenfield projects, those which are moving forward are primarily copper-gold deposits which, in addition to the obvious advantage of the typically counter-cyclical gold revenues, are being driven forward by cash-rich gold miners after more than a year of high gold prices. Also classified here as brownfield and with a greater chance of moving ahead are the mine extensions and expansions through the development of new orebodies, such as the sulphide orebodies at Carmen de Andacollo and Radomiro Tomic in Chile. These projects have the advantages of brownfield projects in that they will use much of the same infrastructure and the same workforces as the existing CRU International Limited confidential 8 Copper Quarterly Report January 2010 Executive Summary ## Total production from new projects to reach nearly 4.4M tonnes by 2014 ‘000t contained copper-in-concentrates and recoverable EW production Data: CRU Analysis © 2010 CRU International Limited confidential
operations, but also carry many of the same risks as greenfield projects and may be subject to similar delays. In 2010, we are forecasting that projects will provide some 420,000t of copper, all of which is from committed projects. Around half of this will be from brownfield expansions and mine restarts, and the remainder from new greenfield projects. Project development is expected to gain momentum as the period progresses, as finance will become easier with global economic recovery and high prices will continue to encourage development in new mine projects. If the current trend to increased Chinese involvement in mining projects continues, this may also accelerate project development

. 

After 2010, the contribution to production from projects is expected to increase by around 1M tonnes per year, and our mine production forecast for 2014 includes nearly 4.4M tonnes from projects.  The proportion from committed projects will decline as the period progresses, as developments become less certain, so that by 2014 about 60% will be from committed projects, mostly brownfield expansions and mine extensions. 

### Balanced market shifting towards deficits by 2014 

For 2010, CRU forecasts a small deficit of almost 200,000 tonnes in the refined cathode market. Copper prices should remain well above the costs of most mines and we expect refined production growth to remain flat this year as a 1% increase in elecro-refined production is offset by a 5% decline in EW production.  As for consumption, we expect Chinese growth to remain strong with modest growth in the world ex-China but from a very low base.  A return of the usual seasonal pattern to consumption should lead to a deficit and higher prices in H1 2010, followed by a return to surplus and lower prices in H2.  As a result, we have raised our copper price forecast for 2010 from $6,350/t to $7,750/t as positive economic news supports strong

investor sentiment and inflows into base metals that lends support to copper.  With prices this high, recycling rates will also rise, but generation rates of new scrap will only show a small recovery in 2010 due to the lower levels of industrial activity in North America and Europe. 

Prices anywhere close to $7,000/t seemed unthinkable this time last year, and as we look ahead we would expect ongoing volatility this year.  A spike in the price to $9,000/t cannot be ruled out.  What is certain, however, is that the gains seen as the year progressed in 2009 are unlikely to play out again in 2010.  It remains to be seen if prices will trade in a sideways fashion, although we believe that the downside risk to prices will be limited by the still relatively low levels of stocks.  Ultimately it is the tightening of Chinese monetary policy that is the key risk to our price and demand forecast. 

SRB restocking at the end of 2008 and early 2009 marked the start of the recovery in copper prices last year.  We doubt there will be a major restocking programme by the SRB during 2010, but acknowledge that their plans are unknown.  It seems unlikely that the SRB would buy any excess cathode at these high prices.  Our assumption is that any significant restocking programme will be delayed until prices retreat significantly from current levels. 

Over the period 2011-2013, supply is expected to grow rapidly at an average rate of 6%, reflecting a combination of production restarts and projects coming on stream.  However, this additional production will still fail to meet the growth in demand for refined copper sufficiently and stocks will be continuously dra

wn down.  This reflects robust refined demand growth supported both by Chinese requirements and a structural shortage of scrap which will support prices around the $7,600/t level in 2011 and 2012.  By 2013 we expect prices to begin to ramp up in anticipation of the market slipping into deficit in 2014.  The high price scenario suggests that substitution becomes a major issue beyond 2012, particularly if the supply side continues to underperform.  We would then expect copper to be rationed out of low value-added applications (mainly non-electrical applications). 

Although China is due to become self sufficient in semis production beyond 2012/13, it will nevertheless remain a net importer of refined copper and, with a global shortfall in production of almost 250,000t in 2014, there is little to prevent prices breaching an average of $8,500/t by the end of our forecast period. 

### Points to watch 

#### **Downside** 



- The main downside threat is from a double-dip recession.  The financial sector in the industrialised world is still fragile as evidenced by the Dubai debt drama that came to light in November 2009. 



- Chinese inflation and monetary tightening could also be overdone, dampening copper demand prospects in this key market. 



- Investors could see more potential upside in the global manufacturing sector during a new upswing.  If copper looks less attractive relative to other alternatives, they could become net sellers. 



- Economisation and substitution – the record gap between copper prices and those of competing materials (especially aluminium) – is not going to go away and will lead to a return of the substitution threat.

- Automotive: scrappage schemes have only brought forward demand from future quarters threatening another mini-boom/bust cycle in 2010 as schemes are unwound. 

- Construction: Lack of credit growth threatens an extended period of weak growth. 



- Should any of the above lead to prices falling, we anticipate the SRB would come back into the market to continue replenishing stocks, thus limiting the downside to any price correction. 

#### **Upside** 



- Chinese control of macroeconomic policy could be insufficient and the momentum built up in 2009 could see a spike in imports and the copper price in the short term, though this would likely be followed by a bust once the brakes are applied more vigorously. 



- The industrialised world could see an earlier economic recovery than forecast, which would see more rapid re-stocking and a jump in the price. 



- Mine underperformance will generally provide support for prices.  Beyond 2010, a return of production growth threatens a return of high capital cost inflation (as during the boom years), as miners scramble to obtain equipment to expand operations.
